en: The Sūtra on the Seal of Entering Samādhi and Non-Entering Samādhi, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, and sixty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Their names were:

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyasamudgata Bodhisattva, and Saṃghagarjitasvararāja Bodhisattva; with these and others as their leaders, all of whom had attained the samādhi of tranquil discernment, the samādhi of the heroic stride, and the samādhi of the profound, immovable ocean tide, and who had accomplished the empowerment dhāraṇī and the dhāraṇī for accomplishing the form-bodies of infinite Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We only pray that the World-Honored One will expound for the sake of all bodhisattvas the Dharma-gate of the Seal of Entering Certainty and Uncertainty. By entering this Dharma-seal, we shall be able to understand and realize it.”
This is an indeterminate bodhisattva who seeks unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, yet may regress from the path of unexcelled wisdom;
this is a determinate bodhisattva who seeks unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and does not regress from the path of unexcelled wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī,
you should know that there are five kinds of practices for bodhisattvas.”
What are these five? They are:

the movement of a sheep-cart, the movement of an elephant-cart, the movement by the supernatural power of the sun and moon deities, the movement by the supernatural power of the śrāvakas, and the movement by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī! These are the five kinds of practices of a bodhisattva. Mañjuśrī!
The first two bodhisattvas are not yet certain regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
the latter three bodhisattvas have attained certainty regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
why is it that bodhisattvas of the two indeterminate types, while seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may regress from the path of unexcelled wisdom?”
"What are the three determinations by which a bodhisattva, seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, does not regress from the path of unexcelled wisdom?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"That which is called 'the movement of a sheep-cart' and 'the movement of an elephant-cart'—these two types of bodhisattvas, while seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, do regress from the path of unexcelled wisdom."

The divine power of the sun and moon, the divine power of the śrāvakas, and the divine power of the Tathāgatas—by means of these three, bodhisattvas seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and do not regress from the path of unexcelled wisdom.
“Mañjuśrī, what is the bodhisattva who travels by sheep-cart?
It is like a person who, for the sake of a great matter or a weighty matter, wishes to pass through worlds as numerous as the atoms in five buddha-fields.”
He reflected to himself:
"By what vehicle shall I now be able to cross over such worlds?
Then he thought this:
"You should ride a sheep-cart and pass through that world. Mañjuśrī!

This person then mounted a sheep-cart and traveled along the road; after enduring great hardship for a long time and traveling a hundred *yojana*, he was suddenly struck by a great wind that blew him back eighty *yojana*.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
Could a person riding that sheep-cart, whether for one eon, a hundred eons, a thousand eons, a hundred million eons, or even unspeakably unspeakable eons, ever transcend a single world-system?
Mañjuśrī replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”

For such a person to ride that sheep-drawn chariot for one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas, or a hundred million kalpas, or even for an unspeakably unspeakable number of kalpas, and yet be able to transcend a single world-system—this is impossible.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"

Mañjuśrī, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having resolved their mind to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, should dwell together with śrāvakas, serve them, draw near to them, become intimate with them, or engage in discussion with them; or if, whether in groves, monasteries, or shared walking paths, they recite, contemplate, and explain the meaning of the teachings of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, or further teach others to recite, contemplate, and explain the meaning of the teachings of the Śrāvaka Vehicle—then because they have upheld the teachings of the Śrāvaka Vehicle and planted roots of goodness therein, their wisdom becomes weak and inferior, and they retreat from the path of unsurpassed wisdom. Although they previously cultivated the bodhicitta and possessed the faculty of wisdom and the eye of wisdom, because they have upheld the teachings of the Śrāvaka Vehicle and planted roots of goodness therein, their faculties become dull, and they consequently fall away and lose the path of unsurpassed wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! Suppose there is a person whose eyes are afflicted by cataracts and closed; wishing to have them opened, he undergoes medical treatment for his eyes for a month until they are healed.
At that time, an enemy takes a handful of finely ground long pepper powder and places it into his eyes, whereupon they once again become closed and dark.
"So it is, so it is! Mañjuśrī!

Although that bodhisattva has previously cultivated the root of wisdom and the eye of wisdom regarding the mind of enlightenment, because he has planted roots of goodness by upholding the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle, his faculties become dull, and he consequently falls away from the path of unsurpassed wisdom."
“Mañjuśrī! This is what is called a bodhisattva who travels by means of a sheep-drawn chariot. Mañjuśrī!”
What is the bodhisattva who travels by elephant chariot?
It is like a person who, for the sake of a great matter or a weighty matter, wishes to pass through as many worlds as there were previously mentioned atoms of dust.
He reflected to himself:
"By what vehicle should I now travel to be able to cross over such worlds?
Then he had this thought:
"I shall mount that supreme and exquisite elephant-chariot, complete with its eight limbs, and cross over to that world. Mañjuśrī!

That person then mounts the elephant-chariot and proceeds along the road; after traveling two thousand yojanas over the course of a hundred years, he is suddenly struck by a great wind that blows him back a thousand yojanas.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think? Could that person,
riding upon that elephant chariot, traverse even a single world-system in one eon, or a hundred eons, or a thousand eons, or a hundred billion eons, or even an unspeakably unspeakable number of eons?
Mañjuśrī replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”

If such a person were to ride that elephant chariot for one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas, or a thousand billion kalpas, or even for unspeakably unspeakable kalpas, and were able to transcend a single world-system, such a thing is impossible.
"So it is, so it is! Mañjuśrī!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family gives rise to the aspiration seeking unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,"
They then dwell together with the śrāvakas, attending upon them, drawing near to them, and becoming familiar through conversation;
they share their enjoyments with them, whether in gardens, within monasteries, or at common places for walking meditation, where they recite, contemplate,
and explain the meaning of the Śrāvaka-yāna teachings, or further instruct others to recite, contemplate, and study the Śrāvaka teachings.

Regarding the Śrāvaka-yāna teachings, one explains their meaning; because one upholds these Śrāvaka-yāna teachings and thereby plants roots of goodness, one’s wisdom becomes weak and inferior, causing one to regress from the path of unsurpassed wisdom.

Although one has previously cultivated the bodhicitta and possesses the faculty of wisdom and the eye of wisdom, nevertheless, due to upholding the Śrāvaka-yāna teachings and planting roots of goodness therein, it causes those faculties—
Being dull-witted, they will immediately fall away from the path of unsurpassed wisdom. Mañjuśrī!
It is like a great log a hundred thousand yojanas long that falls into the great ocean and drifts along with the waves.

There were many yakṣas dwelling in the sky who pulled him toward the great ocean and held him there, further binding him with an iron anvil five thousand yojanas in length and breadth to keep him fixed in place.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
Can this great log cross the great ocean and bring benefit to all sentient beings?
Mañjuśrī replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is! Mañjuśrī!”

Although that bodhisattva cultivates the mind of enlightenment, upholds the Mahāyāna, and plants the roots of all virtues, because they cultivate the dharmas of the śrāvakas, they are pulled back from the ocean of omniscience; they are unable to advance toward the ocean of omniscience, nor can they rescue and deliver all sentient beings within the ocean of birth and death.
"Mañjuśrī! This is what is called a 'bodhisattva who travels by elephant chariot. Mañjuśrī!"
What is the Bodhisattva Sun-Moon Divine Power Practice?
It is, for example, as if there were a person who, for the sake of a great causal condition or a weighty causal condition, wished to pass through worlds as numerous as the aforementioned atoms.
He reflected to himself:
"By what supernormal power (ṛddhi) shall I now be able to transcend such a world?
Then he had this thought:
"I shall employ the supernatural power of the sun and moon to pass beyond that world.
Mañjuśrī! That person then immediately employed the supernatural power of the sun and moon and proceeded along the road.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
Would that person be able to transcend those worlds?
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Such a person would be able to cross over such worlds, yet they would undergo much toil and hardship along the long road.”
The Buddha said, “It is so, Mañjuśrī!”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having resolved their mind to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, does not dwell together with śrāvakas, nor serve, attend upon, or associate with them in conversation; nor does he share with them the use of food or clothing; nor does he stay in groves or monasteries at the same places for walking meditation to recite, study, or contemplate even a single verse of the Śrāvaka-yāna teachings, nor does he instruct others to recite, study, or contemplate the Śrāvaka-yāna teachings;
but constantly and only recites and studies the Mahāyāna, and expounds the Mahāyāna.
"Mañjuśrī! This is called the Bodhisattva Sūryacandraprabhāsa-vikramin. Mañjuśrī!"
What is a bodhisattva who practices through the power of the spiritual penetrations (*ṛddhi*) of a śrāvaka?
It is, for example, like a person who, for the sake of a great matter or a weighty matter, wishes to traverse as many worlds as there are atoms in the aforementioned number.
He reflected to himself:
"By what supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*) should I now be able to transcend such a world?
Then he thought this:
"I shall use the supernatural power of a śrāvaka to pass beyond that world.
And so, he immediately used the supernatural power of a śrāvaka to pass beyond that world. Mañjuśrī!
"What do you think?
Would such a person be able to transcend that world?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This person is able to transcend such worlds.
The Buddha said:
“Just so, just so! Mañjuśrī!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having resolved their mind to seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, does not dwell together with śrāvakas, nor serves, attends upon, or associates with them in conversation; nor shares with them the enjoyment of food and clothing; nor stays in groves or monasteries at the same walking-places to recite, study, or contemplate even a single verse of the Śrāvaka-yāna teachings; nor teaches others to recite, study, or contemplate the Śrāvaka-yāna teachings;”

One should constantly contemplate reading, reciting, and expounding the Mahāyāna; one should give rise to a mind of reverence toward those who have deep faith in the Mahāyāna, read and recite the Mahāyāna, and uphold the Mahāyāna; one should personally attend to, take refuge in, and dwell together with them, serving and drawing near to them, becoming familiar with them, and engaging in discussion with them. One should always seek to receive, uphold, read, and recite the Mahāyāna, further making offerings with a reverent mind using various kinds of incense, flowers, ointments, powdered incense, lamps, and flower garlands. One should constantly contemplate reading and reciting the Mahāyāna sūtras, and joyfully expound them for others.

One should give rise to a mind of reverence toward bodhisattvas who have not yet studied, speaking first with a smile and without coarseness; what one says should be gentle and soft, making it a joy for others to hear, and even if one encounters circumstances that threaten one's life, one shall never abandon the mind of the Mahāyāna.

If there is a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna, recites the Mahāyāna, and upholds the Mahāyāna, one should always give rise to a superior mind toward such a person and make offerings to them; furthermore, one should not engage in disputes or rivalries with others. One should always joyfully seek out Mahāyāna sūtras not yet heard, maintain a respectful mind toward those who preach the Dharma, and regard them as great teachers. One should also give rise to a heart of reverence toward bodhisattvas who have not yet studied. Regarding the faults of others, whether real or unreal, one should not criticize them; nor should one take pleasure in seeking out the failings of others. Instead, one should always delight in practicing loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
"Mañjuśrī! This is called a bodhisattva who practices through the power of the śrāvaka’s spiritual penetrations. Mañjuśrī!"
What is a bodhisattva who practices through the power of the Tathāgata’s spiritual penetrations?
It is like a person who, for the sake of a great purpose or a weighty matter, wishes to pass through as many worlds as there are atoms in the aforementioned number.
He thought to himself:
"What supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*) should I now employ to be able to pass through such worlds so swiftly?
Then he had this thought:
"I shall, by means of the supernatural power of that Tathāgata, transcend that world.
And so, by means of the supernatural power of that Tathāgata, he transcended that world. Mañjuśrī!
"What do you think?
Would such a person be able to transcend that world?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This person will be able to swiftly transcend that world.
The Buddha said:
“Just so, just so! Mañjuśrī!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family resolves to seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should not dwell together with śrāvakas, nor serve, attend upon, or become intimate with them in conversation; nor should they share with them the use of food or clothing. They should not be in the same groves, monasteries, or walking paths as them to read, recite, or contemplate even a single verse of the Śrāvaka vehicle teachings, nor should they instruct others to read, recite, or contemplate the Śrāvaka vehicle teachings.”

They constantly contemplate reading and reciting the Mahāyāna and expounding the Mahāyāna; they always maintain purity of body, speech, and mind, and always abide securely in the precepts and wholesome dharmas; furthermore, they are able to cause others to purify their body, speech, and mind, and to abide securely in the dharma of the precepts.
If there is a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna, recites the Mahāyāna, and upholds the Mahāyāna,
one should always show reverence and take refuge in such a person, serving, attending upon, and associating closely with them in conversation;
sharing all clothing and food together, one should dwell with that bodhisattva and frequent the same places for walking meditation.
Constantly seeking the Mahāyāna, embracing the Mahāyāna, and upholding the Mahāyāna;
making offerings with various kinds of incense, flowers, ointments, powdered incense, lamps, and flower garlands with a reverent mind;
constantly contemplating and reciting the Mahāyāna sūtras; joyfully expounding the Mahāyāna; and toward those who have not yet studied the Bodhi...
He does not give rise to pride, and he causes other bodhisattvas to abide [in it] as well; he speaks with a smile and first addresses others with words that are not coarse or harsh;
what he says is gentle and pleasant for others to hear, and he treats others in this same way.
Even if one encounters circumstances that threaten one's life, one shall not abandon the mind of the Mahāyāna.

If there is a bodhisattva who has set out in the Mahāyāna, recites the Mahāyāna, and upholds the Mahāyāna, they should serve it with a superior mind of joy and reverence, and likewise teach others to honor and make offerings to it. They should not engage in disputes or contention with others; they should always delight in seeking out Mahāyāna sūtras they have not yet heard. Toward those who preach the Dharma, they should give rise to a respectful mind and conceive of them as great teachers. They should not harbor pride toward bodhisattvas who have not yet studied. Regarding the faults of others—whether real or unreal—they should not criticize them, nor should they take pleasure in seeking out the failings of others. Having practiced this themselves, they further teach others to train in this same way.

“Mañjuśrī! In this way, a bodhisattva observes those sentient beings who have lost their bodhisattva activities and instructs them so that they may regain those activities; he is also able to cause others to instruct sentient beings who have lost their bodhisattva activities so that they may regain those activities.

He observes those sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva path and instructs them so that they may attain the path; he is also able to cause others to observe sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva path and instruct them so that they may attain the path.”

One observes oneself and instructs sentient beings who have lost the practice of a bodhisattva so that they may attain it; one also enables others to observe sentient beings who have lost the practice of a bodhisattva and instruct them so that they may attain it.

One observes oneself and instructs sentient beings who have lost the causes of a bodhisattva so that they may attain those causes; one also enables others to observe sentient beings who have lost the causes of a bodhisattva and instruct them so that they may attain those causes.

One observes oneself and instructs sentient beings who have lost the skillful means of a bodhisattva so that they may attain those skillful means; one also enables others to observe sentient beings who have lost the skillful means of a bodhisattva and instruct them so that they may attain those skillful means.

Observing for oneself those sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva’s objective, one teaches them so that they may attain that objective; one is also able to lead others to observe those sentient beings who have lost the bodhisattva’s objective and teach them so that they may attain it.

Observing for oneself those sentient beings who have lost the power of the bodhisattva’s application, one causes them to attain that application; one is also able to lead others to observe those sentient beings who have lost the power of the bodhisattva’s application and cause them to attain it.

Observing for oneself those sentient beings who have lost the basis upon which the bodhisattva’s practice relies, one causes them to attain that basis; one is also able to lead others to observe those sentient beings who have lost the basis upon which the bodhisattva’s practice relies and cause them to attain it.

They personally observe sentient beings who have lost loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and cause them to attain these; they are also able to lead others to observe sentient beings who have lost loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and cause them to attain these.

They personally observe sentient beings who have lost impartial conduct, and cause them to attain impartial conduct; they are also able to lead others to observe sentient beings who have lost impartial conduct, and cause them to attain it.

They personally observe sentient beings who do not place faith in the Triple Gem, and cause them to place faith in the Triple Gem; they are also able to lead others to observe sentient beings who do not place faith in the Triple Gem, and cause them to place faith in it.

He observes himself so as to cause sentient beings who have lost the desire for wholesome dharmas to regain that desire for wholesome dharmas, and he is also able to cause others to observe sentient beings who have lost the desire for wholesome dharmas so that they may regain it;

he observes himself so as to cause sentient beings who are bound and imprisoned to attain liberation, and he is also able to cause others to observe sentient beings who are bound and imprisoned so that they may attain liberation;

he observes himself so as to provide medicine to sentient beings who suffer from illness, and he is also able to cause others to observe sentient beings who suffer from illness so that they may be provided with medicine.

They personally observe sentient beings who have lost the roots of virtue planted by the Buddhas and cause them to regain those roots, and they also enable others to observe such sentient beings and cause them to regain their roots of virtue;
they personally observe sentient beings who lack a refuge and act as a place of refuge for them, and they also enable others to observe such sentient beings and act as a place of refuge for them;
they personally observe sentient beings who have long been asleep and cause them to attain awakening, and they also enable others to observe such sentient beings and cause them to attain awakening.

They personally observe sentient beings born into lowly states and cause them to be reborn in superior places, and they also enable others to observe such sentient beings and cause them to be reborn in superior places;
they personally observe sentient beings who have lost the bodhicitta and cause them to regain it, and they also enable others to observe such sentient beings and cause them to regain the bodhicitta;

they personally observe sentient beings who have lost their footing in the Dharma and cause them to regain that footing, and they also enable others to observe such sentient beings and cause them to regain their footing in the Dharma.

Observing for themselves those sentient beings who have lost the provisions of merit and wisdom, they cause them to obtain those provisions; they are also able to cause others to observe those sentient beings who have lost the provisions of merit and wisdom and cause them to obtain those provisions.

Observing for themselves those sentient beings who have lost faith in the Mahāyāna, they cause them to enter into right faith; they are also able to cause others to observe those sentient beings who have lost faith in the Mahāyāna and cause them to attain right faith.

Observing for themselves those sentient beings who have lost the protection of ethical discipline, they cause them to abide in the protection of ethical discipline; they are also able to cause others to observe those sentient beings who have lost the protection of ethical discipline and cause them to abide in the protection of ethical discipline.

They personally observe sentient beings who have lost the Dharma and its conformity, causing them to attain it; they are also able to cause others to observe sentient beings who have lost the Dharma and its conformity, causing them to attain it.

They personally observe sentient beings who have lost harmonious patience, causing them to attain it; they are also able to cause others to observe sentient beings who have lost harmonious patience, causing them to attain it.

They personally observe sentient beings who have lost tranquility and insight, causing them to abide in tranquility and insight; they are also able to cause others to observe sentient beings who have lost tranquility and insight, causing them to attain tranquility and insight.

Observing for oneself those sentient beings who have lost the diligence of a bodhisattva, one causes them to abide in diligence; one is also able to cause others to observe those sentient beings who have lost the diligence of a bodhisattva and cause them to attain diligence.

Observing for oneself those sentient beings who have lost generosity, self-discipline, and contentment, one causes them to attain generosity and so forth; one is also able to cause others to observe those sentient beings who have lost generosity and so forth and cause them to attain generosity and so forth.

Observing for oneself those sentient beings who have lost mindfulness, wisdom, retention, and practice, one causes them to attain mindfulness and so forth; one is also able to cause others to observe those sentient beings who have lost mindfulness and so forth and cause them to attain mindfulness and so forth.

One observes oneself and causes sentient beings who have lost the path leading to the further shore to find that path; one also enables others to observe sentient beings who have lost the path leading to the further shore and cause them to find it.

One observes oneself and causes sentient beings who are not born into the family of the Buddhas to be born therein; one also enables others to observe sentient beings who are not born into the family of the Buddhas and cause them to be born therein.

One observes oneself and causes sentient beings who have lost virtuous friends to obtain them; one also enables others to observe sentient beings who have lost virtuous friends and cause them to obtain them.

One observes for oneself those sentient beings who have lost the mind that seeks the benefit of sentient beings and causes them to attain that mind; one is also able to cause others to observe those sentient beings who have lost the mind that seeks the benefit of sentient beings and cause them to attain that mind.

One observes for oneself those sentient beings who have lost reliance upon the Dharma and causes them to attain reliance upon the Dharma; one is also able to cause others to observe those sentient beings who have lost reliance upon the Dharma and cause them to attain reliance upon the Dharma.

One observes for oneself those sentient beings who have lost reliance upon wisdom and causes them to attain reliance upon wisdom; one is also able to cause others to observe those sentient beings who have lost reliance upon wisdom and cause them to attain reliance upon wisdom.

He observes himself so that sentient beings who have lost the meaning of relying [upon the Dharma] may attain the meaning of relying upon it, and he is also able to cause others to observe so that sentient beings who have lost the meaning of relying may attain the meaning of relying;

he observes himself so that sentient beings who have lost reliance on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) may attain reliance on sūtras of definitive meaning, and he is also able to cause others to observe so that sentient beings who have lost reliance on sūtras of definitive meaning may attain reliance on sūtras of definitive meaning;

he observes himself so that sentient beings who have lost the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) may attain the four right efforts, and he is also able to cause others to observe so that sentient beings who have lost the four right efforts may attain the four right efforts.

Observing oneself, one sees sentient beings who have lost truthful speech, Dharma-speech, beneficial speech, and speech that tames; one causes them to abide in truthful speech, Dharma-speech, beneficial speech, and speech that tames. Furthermore, one is able to cause others to observe sentient beings who have lost truthful speech, Dharma-speech, beneficial speech, and speech that tames, and cause them to abide in truthful speech, Dharma-speech, beneficial speech, and speech that tames.

Observing oneself, one sees sentient beings who are poor and lowly and causes them to attain wealth and honor; furthermore, one is able to cause others to observe sentient beings who are poor and lowly and cause them to attain wealth and honor.
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to a mind of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, pervading them all completely, and forms this thought:

‘Those sentient beings have no support and no protector; they have no refuge and no resort; they have no island and no shore; they have no home and no savior. At what time shall I be able to act as a savior for these sentient beings?’”
"Mañjuśrī! For example, just as the youthful and magnificent Garuḍa king, possessing great power, flies at will to the summit of Mount Sumeru;

so too is it with the Tathāgata’s bodhisattva who practices through spiritual power. Endowed with the force of great roots of goodness and swift vigor, he can, according to his will, proceed to be born within the assemblies of Buddhas, and is able to act as a protector for sentient beings in the evil realms."
Mañjuśrī! This is called the bodhisattva Tathāgata-ṛddhivikrāmin. Mañjuśrī!

If a son or daughter of good family were, day after day, to provide offerings of celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors to as many Buddhas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and furthermore, were to practice such giving with wish-fulfilling jewels filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges;

yet if another person were to instruct a single sentient being to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.
“Mañjuśrī! If a son or daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds throughout the ten directions, to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer;
and if another person were to instruct a single sentient being to attain the fruit of a once-returner, the latter’s merit would surpass the former’s by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, to attain the fruit of a Once-Returner;
and if another person were to instruct a single sentient being to attain the fruit of a Non-Returner, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”
“Mañjuśrī! If a son or daughter of good family were to teach all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds of the ten directions, to attain the fruit of a non-returner;
and if another person were to teach a single sentient being to attain the fruit of an arhat, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable degree.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, to attain the fruit of arhatship;

and if another person were to instruct a single sentient being to realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, to attain the fruit of a pratyekabuddha;

and if another person were to instruct a single bodhisattva who travels by sheep-cart to cause them to abide securely in the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former, being immeasurable and incalculable.”
“Mañjuśrī! If a son or daughter of good family were to teach all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds of the ten directions, to attain the bodhicitta that proceeds by sheep-cart;

and if another person were to teach a single sentient being to attain the bodhicitta that proceeds by elephant-cart, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former, being immeasurable and incalculable.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all worlds throughout the ten directions, to attain the bodhicitta of the elephant-cart vehicle;

and if another person were to instruct a single sentient being to attain the bodhicitta of the sun-and-moon-divine-power vehicle, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former by immeasurable and incalculable degrees.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, to attain the bodhicitta of the power of the sun and moon deities;

and if another person were to teach a single sentient being to attain the bodhicitta of the power of the śrāvakas, the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, to attain the bodhicitta of the power of the śrāvaka’s spiritual practice;

and if another person were to teach a single sentient being to attain the bodhicitta of the power of the Tathāgata’s spiritual practice, the latter’s merit would surpass the former’s by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son or daughter of good family were, day after day, to provide offerings of celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors to as many sentient beings as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, continuing such offerings for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;

and if another person were to give a single meal to a single lay follower—one who has taken refuge in the Three Jewels, received the five precepts, and conceived right faith in the Buddha’s teachings—the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former by immeasurable and incalculable degrees.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide offerings of celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors to as many upāsakas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, continuing such offerings for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
and if another person were to give a single meal to one who has attained the eighth stage, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to offer divine fine garments and divine food of a hundred flavors to as many ‘eighth-person’ practitioners as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue making such offerings for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges;
yet if another person were to give a single meal to a single stream-enterer, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide offerings of celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors to as many stream-enterers (srotāpanna) as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue such offerings for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;

yet if another person were to give a single meal to each of those who have attained the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable degree.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to offer divine fine garments and divine food of a hundred flavors to as many once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin) as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue such offerings for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges;
yet if another person were to give a single meal to a single non-returner (anāgāmin), the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son or daughter of good family were to provide offerings of celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors to as many non-returners (anāgāmin) as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue such offerings for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges;
yet if another person were to give a single meal to a single arhat (arhan), the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by immeasurable and incalculable degrees.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son or daughter of good family were to offer divine fine garments and divine food of a hundred flavors to as many Arhats as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue such offerings for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
yet if another person were to give a single meal to a single Pratyekabuddha, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide offerings of celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors to as many Pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, continuing such offerings for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
and if another person were to give a single meal to a single Bodhisattva who travels by sheep-cart—the latter’s merit would surpass that of the former, being immeasurable and incalculable.”
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!

Whenever and for whatever reason this bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the mind of enlightenment, at that very moment there is not a single unwholesome thing that is not abandoned, and not a single Buddha-dharma that does not grow.
Mañjuśrī! Because a bodhisattva is endowed with such inconceivable and supreme merits, Mañjuśrī!

It is, for example, like the king of birds, the kalaviṅka, who, while still within its eggshell and though it has not yet hatched, already surpasses all other flocks of birds because it possesses a profound, wondrous, and beautiful voice.
"So it is, so it is! Mañjuśrī!

Although a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening remains within the shell of ignorance and is obscured by the dark veil of karma and afflictions, they are nonetheless superior to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, because they possess the wondrous sound of the roots of goodness, practices, and vows dedicated toward enlightenment."

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide offerings of celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors to as many Bodhisattvas practicing on sheep-carts as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue such offerings for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;

yet if another person were to give a single meal to a single Bodhisattva practicing on an elephant-cart, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide offerings of celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors to as many elephant-caravan Bodhisattvas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, and were to continue such offerings for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;

yet if another person were to give a single meal to a single Bodhisattva of Solar-Lunar Divine Power Practice, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to offer celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors to as many bodhisattvas who practice with divine power as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, continuing such offerings for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;

yet if another person were to give a single meal to a single śrāvaka who practices with divine power, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable degree.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide offerings of celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors to as many śrāvakas and bodhisattvas of spiritual power as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, continuing such offerings for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges;

and if another person were to give a single meal to a single tathāgata-bodhisattva of spiritual power, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide offerings of celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors to as many Tathāgatas and Śrāvakas as there are atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions, continuing such offerings for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges;
yet if another person, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, were to believe and accept it with a profound mind, their merit would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.”
“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to construct monasteries as numerous as the atoms in all the worlds of the ten directions,
and were to provide offerings to as many pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, and [provide] their monastic dwellings...”
All were fashioned from Jambūnada gold and adorned with lightning-lamp maṇi jewels;
all kinds of luminous gems formed their steps, while maṇis, pearls, various treasures, and necklaces served as their ornaments;
banners, canopies, silken streamers, and pennants were suspended and arrayed everywhere, along with the king of wish-fulfilling jewels.
...with jeweled nets and bells forming its canopy; with dragon-guarded sandalwood used as fragrant mud to smear the ground;
and with *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, *mañjūṣaka*, *mahāmañjūṣaka*, *sumana*, *utpala*, and *kumuda* flowers.
He scattered various supreme and exquisite flowers, such as the *śirīṣa*, *puṇḍarīka*,
*pāriyātra*, *tārṇaka*, *gotārṇaka*, *varṣika*, and *sugandhika* flowers;
he made offerings with celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors, and then—
If one were to provide such offerings for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;

yet if another person were to hear the name of the Buddha, or the name of the Omniscient One, or the name of the Lord of the World, or even behold an image, or any painted depiction within a scripture—the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.
How much more so for a person who joins their ten fingers and toes in reverence; their merit surpasses that of the former, being immeasurable and incalculable.

How much more so for one who offers various lamps, incense, and flowers, or even praises a single mark of the Buddha’s merit; their merit becomes even more superior, such that they shall enjoy great wealth and happiness in future lives, until they reach the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
“Mañjuśrī! Just as a single drop of water cast into the great ocean will never be exhausted until the time the kalpa-fire arises; Mañjuśrī!”
So it is with the bodhisattva: by dedicating even a small root of virtue toward the attainment of buddhahood, it never reaches its end until the fire of omniscience arises. Mañjuśrī!
For example, just as the lunar disk surpasses all the stars with its full, vast, and sublime radiance, so too is the bodhisattva:
by dedicating even a small root of virtue toward the attainment of Buddhahood, they surpass those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, because their roots of virtue are vast and sublime.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses such inconceivable merits as these. Mañjuśrī!

If a son or daughter of good family were to provide celestial fine garments and celestial food of a hundred flavors as offerings to all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas in worlds as numerous as the atoms of all the ten directions, continuing such offerings for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges;

yet if another person were able to give rise to faith and acceptance toward this sutra, their merit would surpass that of the former by immeasurable and incalculable amounts—how much more so for one who copies it down or expounds it for others, whose merit is most supreme.
Why is this? Because it is the cause for attaining Buddhahood. "O Mañjuśrī!
If there are men or women who, with a mind of hatred and malice, plunder the food, drink, clothing, and robes of immeasurable śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

and if there are others who, with a mind of hatred and malice, plunder even a small amount of food, drink, clothing, or robes from a bodhisattva who has faith and delight in the Mahāyāna, or cause them to go without food for even a single day, their sin is infinitely and incalculably greater than the former.

Why is this? All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of the three periods of time practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for incalculable eons solely for the sake of severing their own afflictions;
the bodhisattva is not like this, for even when giving as little as a hair’s breadth to an animal, it is all for the sake of ensuring that the Three Jewels are never severed.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were someone who, with a mind of malice and hatred, destroyed the immeasurable, boundless, and innumerable precepts, concentrations, wisdoms, liberations, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of countless Pratyekabuddhas;

and suppose there were another person who, with a mind of malice and hatred, impaired the branches of morality and the points of training of a single Bodhisattva who has faith and joy in the Mahāyāna, causing them not to be accomplished—the latter’s transgression is more grave than the former’s immeasurable and innumerable [transgressions].”

Why is this? Because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas throughout the three periods of time, during incalculable eons, have cultivated all their morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation solely for the purpose of severing the afflictions of their own selves;

the bodhisattva is not like this, for even if they cultivate morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation for only a single day, it is entirely for the purpose of severing the afflictions of sentient beings.
"Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were someone who, with a mind of malice and hatred, bound all sentient beings of the ten directions and cast them into prison;

yet, if another person, with a mind of malice and hatred, would not even look upon a bodhisattva but turned their back and departed, the latter's transgression would be immeasurable and incalculable times greater than the former."
“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were someone who, with a mind of malice and hatred, plucked out the eyes of all sentient beings in all the worlds of the ten directions;

yet, if another person, with a mind of malice and hatred, would not even look at a bodhisattva but turned their back and departed, the latter’s transgression would be immeasurable and incalculable times greater than the former.”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings in the ten directions were to have their eyes plucked out, and another person, conceiving a heart of great compassion toward those beings, were to restore their sight;
the merit obtained by that person would be surpassed by the immeasurable and incalculable merit of one who, with a pure mind, goes to behold a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva.”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were someone who could cause all prisoners throughout the ten directions to attain liberation and experience the pleasures of a Wheel-Turning Sage King or Śakra, Lord of the Devas;
yet if another person, with a pure mind, gazes upon and praises a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by immeasurable and incalculable degrees.”
“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were someone who could cause all sentient beings throughout the ten directions to realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha;

yet if another person were to instruct a single bodhisattva who delights in the Mahāyāna, causing even a single root of goodness planted before a Buddha to increase, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable degree.”

“Mañjuśrī! If there is a bodhisattva with deep faith in the Mahāyāna who causes all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions to abide in the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), the merit thereby obtained is surpassed by that of another person who teaches even a single verse of the Mahāyāna Dharma to others; the latter’s merit is immeasurable and incalculable.”
“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were someone who cast as many Pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals;

yet if another person were to create an obstacle for even a single person who has first resolved to attain Bodhicitta, the latter’s transgression would be immeasurably and infinitely more grave than the former.”
“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were someone who created obstacles for all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions who had resolved their minds upon awakening;

yet if another person were to create an obstacle for the bodhicitta of even a single bodhisattva who has deep faith in the Mahāyāna, the latter’s transgression would be immeasurable and incalculable compared to the former.”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose all sentient beings in the ten directions were to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and the domain of King Yama; and suppose there were someone who rescued them and established them in the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

If another person were to cause even a single sentient being to give rise to deep faith and understanding in the Mahāyāna, the merit of this latter person would surpass that of the former by immeasurable and incalculable amounts.”
“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were someone who, toward as many Pratyekabuddhas as would fill the worlds of the ten directions, gave rise to a mind of contempt;

yet if another person were to give rise to a mind of contempt toward a single Bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment, the latter’s transgression would be immeasurable and incalculable compared to the former.”

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were someone who deprived as many pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions of their offerings and livelihoods, and spread their ill repute throughout the worlds of the ten directions;

yet, if another person were to deprive a single bodhisattva who has deep faith in the Mahāyāna of their offerings and livelihoods, and spread their ill repute, the latter’s transgression would be immeasurable and incalculable times more serious than the former.”

“Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of seeking the true Dharma, were to give even a single water jar to a single bodhisattva who has deep faith in the Mahāyāna, by virtue of this meritorious karma, they shall obtain the immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous fruit of becoming a universal monarch (cakravartin); how much more so when giving to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who upholds, recites, and develops profound faith and understanding?”

When the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra, the youth Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the assembly of śrāvakas, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, humans, and non-humans were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Seal of Entering Samādhi and Non-Entering Samādhi, carved by imperial decree at the Goryeo State Great Canon Bureau in the year of Gui Mao.
